Whole file: -stats + cache API/resolveCodexUrl/resolveCodexWebSocketUrl/parseErrorResponse/extractAccountId/createCodexRequestId/buildBaseCodexHeaders/buildSSEHeaders/buildWebSocketHeaders/codexUsageLimitMessage/resolveCodexServiceTier/applyServiceTierPricing/normalizeCodexStatus. reqwest only. One gap: no WebSocket crate exists in the workspace, so the socket comes from set_web_socket_constructor (None by default). With no constructor connectWebSocket fails with the exact TS message 'WebSocket transport is not available in this runtime', which drives the real fallback path (diagnostic + recordWebSocketFailure + recordWebSocketSseFallback) and then SSE. mapCodexEvents throws via an Arc<Mutex<Option<CodexThrown>>> slot because a Rust stream cannot reject; the caller re-raises it at the same point in the catch boundary.

honest_summary: openai_responses_shared.rs, openai_responses.rs and openai_codex_responses.rs are complete 1:1 ports with unit tests (parsing, serialisation, ordering, error mapping, thresholds, header building, defaults, cached-context delta, fallback diagnostics) and no real network calls. azure_openai_responses.rs is only the helper half: the lead reassigned it while I was writing it, so I stopped rather than merge two authors into one file. The one real functional gap is the WebSocket transport in the Codex provider: there is no WebSocket dependency in the workspace, so the socket is injectable and defaults to 'unavailable', which reproduces the TypeScript's no-WebSocket runtime path exactly (same error message, same reconnect/fallback bookkeeping) and lands on SSE. I could not run cargo check or cargo test (lead builds once at the end), so the files are unverified by a compiler.
